questions.prompt: What is the Python REPL, and how does it differ from running a saved .py script?
options: An interactive prompt where each line runs immediately and nothing is saved once the terminal closes — different from a saved script, which can be rerun the same way every time
A separate compiler that converts Python into machine code before running it
A text editor built into Python specifically for writing .py files
A testing framework that automatically runs every function in a script
A tool that only works with numeric calculations, not strings or print statements
An older version of Python that has been replaced by script-based execution
questions.explain: The REPL (Read-Eval-Print Loop) is the interactive prompt you get by typing `python` with no file — each line runs immediately, but nothing is saved once you close the terminal. A real pipeline needs to run unattended and the same way every time, which is why it has to live in a saved .py script run with `python filename.py`.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B is the closest-sounding wrong answer because it describes something real about how code becomes runnable — but Python has no separate compile step at all. The interpreter reads and runs Python code directly, whether that code came from the REPL or a saved script; there's no machine-code compilation stage to speak of.

questions.code:
quantity_from_file = "2"
unit_price = 129.99

line_total = quantity_from_file * unit_price
print(line_total)
questions.prompt: What happens when this code runs?
options: A TypeError is raised, because Python won't implicitly multiply a string by a float — quantity_from_file must be converted with int() first
It prints 259.98, because Python automatically converts the numeric-looking string to a number
It prints "22222222222222222222222222..." (the string repeated 129 times, truncating the decimal)
It prints 2.0, silently ignoring unit_price entirely
questions.explain: A value read from a file arrives as a string even when it looks like a number. Python won't silently guess what you meant when you multiply a str by a float — it raises a TypeError. The fix is to convert explicitly first: `int(quantity_from_file) * unit_price`, which correctly gives 259.98.

questions.prompt: Given `line_totals = [259.98, 249.50, 79.00, 129.99]`, fill in the blank: `line_totals[________]` returns the last element, 129.99, without needing to know the list's length ahead of time.
questions.explain: A list is indexed by position starting at 0. Python also supports negative indices counting backward from the end, so index -1 always refers to the last element, no matter how long the list is — exactly the pattern used throughout this course for grabbing 'the most recent one.'

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about lists, tuples, and sets in Python, per Chapter 1.
options: A list is ordered and mutable — items can be added, removed, or changed after creation
A tuple can be modified in place after it's created, the same way a list can
A set automatically removes duplicate values and has no guaranteed order
len(set(customer_ids)) counts the number of distinct values, which can be smaller than len(customer_ids)
A tuple is commonly used to return more than one value from a function
Sets preserve the order items were added in, the same way lists do
questions.explain: Lists are ordered and mutable; tuples look similar but are immutable once created — trying to reassign `order_record[0]` raises a TypeError. Sets drop duplicates and have no guaranteed order, which is exactly why `len(set(customer_ids))` (distinct customers) can be smaller than `len(customer_ids)` (total orders). Tuples are the natural way to return more than one value from a function, as in `return min(values), max(values)`.

questions.prompt: Match each control-flow keyword to what it actually does inside a loop.
right: Exits the loop immediately, regardless of its condition
Skips the rest of the current iteration and moves to the next item
Checked only if the preceding if condition was False
Produces 0 through n-1, for looping a fixed number of times
questions.explain: continue jumps straight to the next iteration, skipping whatever code comes after it for the current item. break exits the loop entirely, with no further checks. elif is only reached if every condition before it was False. range(n) produces 0 through n-1 — n values, never reaching n itself — for looping a fixed number of times.

questions.prompt: What does this print?
options: False invalid quantity
False status is Shipped
True None
An error, because validate_order only returns a single value
questions.explain: validate_order checks quantity first: since row["quantity"] is -1, which is <= 0, it returns (False, "invalid quantity") immediately and never reaches the status check at all. is_valid, reason = ... unpacks that tuple into the two variables, so the print statement shows False invalid quantity.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: a list comprehension is written as `[expr for item in collection if condition]` — the part that comes first, before the word "for", is the ________ applied to each item that passes the filter.
questions.explain: A comprehension states its transformation first: `[row["order_id"] for row in orders if row["status"] == "Shipped"]` reads as 'give me row["order_id"]' — the expression — for each row that passes the if condition. The loop variable, collection, and filter come after it, in that order.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about local and global scope in Python, per Lesson 9.
options: A variable created inside a function is destroyed once the function returns
Reading a global variable from inside a function works fine without any special keyword
Modifying a global variable from inside a function is the preferred style used throughout this course
The better habit is to have a function return a value and let the caller decide what to do with it
Two different functions can't both use a local variable with the same name
questions.explain: A local variable like line_total exists only while its function runs and disappears once it returns. Reading a global (like tax_rate) from inside a function needs no special keyword. But modifying a global from inside a function is specifically called out as a bug-prone pattern to avoid — the better habit this course uses throughout is returning a value and letting the caller decide what to do with it. Because locals are scoped to their own function, two different functions can absolutely both use a variable named the same thing internally without conflict.

questions.code:
def summarize_order(row):
    total = round(row["quantity"] * row["unit_price"], 2)
    is_valid = row["quantity"] > 0
    return row["order_id"], total, is_valid

order_id, total = summarize_order({"order_id": 1006, "quantity": 4, "unit_price": 22.00})
questions.prompt: What happens when this code runs?
options: A ValueError is raised, because summarize_order returns a 3-value tuple but only 2 variables are given to unpack it into
order_id becomes 1006 and total becomes the tuple (88.0, True), with no error
It runs fine, silently discarding is_valid
It prints 1006 88.0 True, the same as using all three variables
questions.explain: summarize_order returns a 3-value tuple: (order_id, total, is_valid). Unpacking a tuple requires exactly as many variables on the left as there are values in the tuple — giving it only 2 variables for 3 values raises a ValueError ("too many values to unpack"), it doesn't just drop the extra one or shove it somewhere.

questions.prompt: Match each term from Lessons 9 and 11 to what it actually means.
right: Defined at the top level of a script; readable (but shouldn't usually be modified) from inside a function
`{key: value for item in collection if condition}` — builds a new dictionary in one line
Exists only inside the function where it's created, and is destroyed when the function returns
`[expr for item in collection if condition]` — builds a new list in one line
questions.explain: A local variable lives and dies with the function call it's created in. A global variable, defined at the top level, can be read (but shouldn't usually be modified) from inside a function. A list comprehension builds a new list with `[expr for item in collection if condition]`; a dict comprehension builds a new dict with the same shape, using `{key: value for item in collection if condition}`.

questions.prompt: What does this print?
options: Skipping: Negative quantity (-1) on order 1014
-22.0, because int("-1") doesn't raise an error on its own
An uncaught ValueError, because the except block only catches TypeError
Skipping: invalid literal for int(), because "-1" can't be converted
questions.explain: int("-1") parses fine — a negative quantity is numerically valid, just logically wrong. The function's own `raise ValueError(...)` is what turns that business-rule problem into an exception on purpose, and it's caught by the same `except ValueError` block, printing the message built into the raised error: "Skipping: Negative quantity (-1) on order 1014".

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: calling `raise ValueError(...)` inside your own validation logic lets a business-rule problem (like a negative quantity) plug into the exact same `except ________` block that would also catch a genuine type-conversion failure.
questions.explain: Both a malformed numeric string (int("N/A")) and a deliberately raised business-rule error can be caught by the same except ValueError block, because raise lets your own validation logic plug into Python's normal exception-handling machinery instead of needing separate if/continue checks scattered through the loop.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about calling GitHub's REST API with requests, per Lessons 17 and 18.
options: A 404 response is a normal, well-formed JSON body, not a Python exception raised automatically
response.raise_for_status() raises requests.HTTPError on a 4xx or 5xx response
A pagination loop following response.links should keep going as long as 'next' is still in that dict
Unauthenticated requests to GitHub's API have no rate limit at all
response.json() parses the response body into a Python dict or list
questions.explain: A typo'd URL gets a normal 404 JSON body back, not a raised exception — code that reaches into it without checking will crash with a confusing KeyError instead. raise_for_status() is what turns a 4xx/5xx into a requests.HTTPError. A pagination loop checks for 'next' in response.links and stops once it's gone. response.json() parses the body into Python objects. Unauthenticated GitHub requests are capped at 60/hour per IP — there is a real rate limit, not none at all.

questions.prompt: What makes this loop stop requesting new pages?
options: 'next' is no longer a key in response.links once the final page is reached, so url is set to None
The loop always stops after exactly 100 contributors, matching per_page
params is set to None on the first page, which immediately ends the loop
requests.get() raises an error automatically once there are no more pages
questions.explain: response.links is a dict keyed by relation name ('next', 'last', ...). On the final page, GitHub simply stops including a 'next' entry — that's the condition this loop checks. Once 'next' is missing, url is set to None, and `while url:` stops the loop, with no hardcoded page count needed.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of paginating through a GitHub API endpoint using response.links, per Lesson 18, in the correct order.
items: Send a GET request for the current page, with per_page and page (or the full next URL) as parameters
Call response.raise_for_status() and add the current page's results to the running list
Check whether 'next' is a key in response.links
If it is, set url to that next URL and continue the loop; if not, set url to None and stop
questions.explain: Each pass through the loop requests the current page, validates and collects its results, then checks response.links for a 'next' entry to decide whether to keep going or stop — exactly the order Lesson 18's loop follows, with no hardcoded page count anywhere in it.

questions.prompt: orders.csv has 20 rows and 10 columns, including order 1014's quantity of -1. What does this print?
options: (20, 10) then int64
(20, 10) then object, because pandas can't infer a type on a column containing a negative value
(19, 10) then int64, because pandas drops the invalid negative-quantity row automatically
An error, because -1 isn't a valid quantity
questions.explain: df.shape is (rows, columns) — 20 orders, 10 columns, matching the file exactly. Pandas infers quantity as a real int64 column, because -1 is a perfectly valid integer. Pandas infers type, not correctness — it does not flag or drop a negative quantity on its own; finding that kind of business-rule problem is still the engineer's job (Lesson 22).

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: `df.isna()` returns a same-shaped DataFrame of True/False values; calling `.________()` on that result counts how many True values (missing values) are in each column.
questions.explain: df.isna() marks every cell True/False for whether it's missing. Chaining .sum() on top of that adds up the True values per column, which is exactly how Lesson 22 finds the single missing customer_name (order 1005) in orders.csv.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about cleaning orders.csv in Chapter 4, per Lesson 22.
options: df.duplicated(subset=["customer_name"]) flags rows as duplicates just because the same customer placed more than one real order
.fillna(value) replaces every NaN in a column with value, keeping the row
df.isna() catches order 1014's negative quantity, since -1 is treated as missing
.dropna(subset=["customer_name"]) would remove order 1005 entirely instead of keeping it with a placeholder name
df.duplicated(subset=["order_id"]) finds 7 duplicate rows in orders.csv
questions.explain: Checking duplicated(subset=["customer_name"]) flags 7 rows, but that's customers like Dana Whitfield legitimately placing 3 separate real orders, not accidental duplicates — checking subset=["order_id"] instead finds 0, the correct answer for this dataset. .fillna() keeps the row and replaces its missing value; .dropna(subset=...) would have removed order 1005 entirely, losing otherwise-good data. A negative quantity isn't a missing value at all, so isna() never flags it — it needs its own explicit check.

questions.prompt: Run against the unfiltered orders.csv (before removing the cancelled and returned rows), what does the Footwear row of total_revenue show, and why?
options: $909.93 — groupby() summarizes whatever rows it's handed, including the cancelled and returned Footwear orders that haven't been filtered out yet
$649.95 — groupby() automatically excludes Cancelled and Returned rows before aggregating
$0.00 — groupby() can't aggregate a column before duplicates are removed
An error — agg() requires the data to already be filtered to valid rows
questions.explain: groupby() has no idea which rows are 'bad' — it just aggregates whatever is handed to it. Run against the unfiltered data, Footwear's total_revenue includes the cancelled order 1004 and returned order 1008, totaling $909.93. Only after filtering to status == "Shipped" and quantity >= 0 first does the clean total drop to $649.95 — deciding which rows belong in the summary is the engineer's job, not groupby()'s.

questions.prompt: Match each df.merge() how= option to what it actually keeps, per Lesson 25.
right: Only rows whose key matched on both sides — can silently drop unmatched rows with no NaN warning
Every row from both DataFrames, matched or not, filling NaN wherever there's no match
Every row from the calling (left) DataFrame — unmatched rows get NaN in the new columns
Every row from the other (right) DataFrame
questions.explain: how="left" keeps every row from the calling DataFrame, filling NaN where there's no match on the right. how="inner" keeps only rows matching on both sides — the real danger, since it can silently drop rows with no NaN to warn you. how="right" keeps every row from the other DataFrame instead. how="outer" keeps every row from both sides, NaNs and all.

questions.prompt: Lesson 24 shows that grouping before filtering can include rows that shouldn't count. Put these steps in the correct order for computing a clean, accurate per-category revenue total from orders.csv.
items: Load orders.csv into a DataFrame and compute each row's line_total
Filter to only rows where status == "Shipped" and quantity >= 0
Group the filtered DataFrame by category
Sum line_total within each group to get the clean per-category revenue
questions.explain: Filter-then-group, not group-then-filter: computing line_total first, removing the cancelled/returned/negative-quantity rows next, and only then grouping and summing is what gives Footwear's real $649.95 instead of the unfiltered $909.93 that still includes rows that shouldn't count.

questions.prompt: In a pyodbc connection string, what does `Trusted_Connection=yes` actually do?
options: Uses Windows authentication to connect, instead of a SQL Server username and password
Encrypts the connection using TLS
Tells SQL Server to trust any client certificate presented
Automatically retries the connection if it fails
Grants the connecting account administrator privileges on the database
Disables the need to specify a DATABASE name
questions.explain: A pyodbc connection string has four pieces: DRIVER, SERVER, DATABASE, and the authentication method. Trusted_Connection=yes picks Windows authentication for that last piece, instead of supplying a UID and PWD for SQL Server authentication.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B is the closest-sounding wrong answer because it also concerns connection security — but Trusted_Connection is specifically about which authentication method is used (Windows identity vs. a SQL login), not about whether the connection's traffic is encrypted. Encryption is a separate connection-string setting entirely.

questions.code:
cursor.execute(
    "INSERT INTO Staging.ProductSnapshot (ProductName) VALUES (?);",
    ("Untracked Row",)
)
conn.close()
questions.prompt: conn.commit() was never called before conn.close(). What happens to the inserted row?
options: It's rolled back and never actually written, because pyodbc connections aren't in autocommit mode by default
It's written permanently, because execute() commits automatically
It raises an error on close() because of the uncommitted transaction
It's written, but only visible to the same connection, never to other sessions
questions.explain: By default, pyodbc connections are not in autocommit mode — every INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE sits inside an open transaction until conn.commit() is called. Closing the connection without committing silently discards the work, which is deliberate: it's exactly what lets you roll back a bad write before committing.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: in pyodbc, a query like `"SELECT * FROM Production.Product WHERE Name = ?;"` uses a ________ placeholder, whose actual value is sent to SQL Server separately from the SQL text itself.
questions.explain: The ? placeholder is pyodbc's parameter marker. The value passed alongside it (via params= or as a tuple) is sent to SQL Server as a value, never spliced into the SQL text — which is exactly what prevents it from ever being interpreted as SQL syntax, even if it contains something like a quote character.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about SQL injection and parameterized queries, per Lesson 29.
options: Building a query with an f-string and splicing in a variable can let attacker-controlled text become attacker-controlled SQL
A parameterized query sends a value like O'Brien's Gear correctly, even though it contains an apostrophe
Parameterization is only a security concern — it has no effect on correctness for ordinary values
Any value that comes from a variable, file, API response, or user input belongs in a parameter, not spliced into the SQL string
A '?' placeholder is parsed by SQL Server as part of the SQL syntax, the same as a spliced-in string would be
questions.explain: An f-string query with a malicious spliced-in value can turn into two statements, one of them destructive — that's SQL injection. A parameter also sidesteps real formatting bugs, like an apostrophe in O'Brien's Gear breaking a hand-built query string, because it's never treated as SQL syntax at all — so parameterization is about correctness too, not only security. The rule given is that any non-literal value belongs in a parameter. A ? placeholder's value is sent separately from the SQL text, never parsed as SQL syntax itself.

questions.prompt: Match each df.to_sql() if_exists option to what it actually does, per Lesson 30.
right: Raises an error if the table already exists
Adds the DataFrame's rows to an existing table
Drops the existing table and recreates it from the DataFrame
questions.explain: "append" adds rows to an existing table without touching what's already there. "replace" drops and recreates the table first, from the DataFrame. "fail", the default, raises an error if the table already exists at all — forcing a deliberate choice instead of silently overwriting or duplicating data.

questions.prompt: orders.csv has 20 rows: one (order 1005) with a missing customer_name, and one (order 1014) with a negative quantity. What does this print?
options: Loaded 18 rows (from 20 extracted).
Loaded 20 rows (from 20 extracted).
Loaded 18 rows (from 18 extracted).
Loaded 19 rows (from 20 extracted).
questions.explain: extract() reads all 20 rows unchanged. transform() drops the row missing customer_name (dropna) and the row with quantity <= 0 (the quantity > 0 filter), leaving 18. load() writes those 18 and returns 18, while len(raw_df) — the original extracted count — is still 20, so the message reads "Loaded 18 rows (from 20 extracted)."

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: a ________ is the highest value of an ordering column (usually a date) that's already been successfully loaded — the next pipeline run only extracts rows after it, instead of reloading everything.
questions.explain: A watermark is just the highest already-loaded value of an ordering column like order_date. The next run compares new rows' order_date against it, extracting only what's newer — exactly how Lesson 36 avoids re-extracting and re-loading an entire dataset on every run.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about idempotency and upserts, per Lesson 37.
options: A pipeline step is idempotent if running it twice with the same input produces the same result as running it once
if_exists="append" has no way of knowing the data was already loaded, so running it twice doubles the row count
INSERT OR REPLACE in SQLite inserts a row if its primary key doesn't exist yet, and replaces it in place if it does
Making the Load step idempotent means you must figure out exactly which rows loaded before a crash before it's safe to rerun
questions.explain: Idempotency means a step run twice has the same effect as running it once. if_exists="append" blindly appends every time, so running it twice against the same 18-row batch produces 36 rows, 18 of them exact duplicates. INSERT OR REPLACE, keyed on a primary key like order_id, is SQLite's upsert — insert if new, replace if it already exists. Because load_upsert() is idempotent, the whole point is that recovery doesn't require figuring out exactly which rows made it in before a crash — rerunning the full batch simply re-upserts everything with no duplicates.

questions.code:
def load_append_only(df, db_path="orders_warehouse.db"):
    conn = sqlite3.connect(db_path)
    df.to_sql("orders", conn, if_exists="append", index=False)
    conn.close()

load_append_only(clean_df)   # clean_df has 18 rows
load_append_only(clean_df)   # run again
questions.prompt: What's in the orders table after both calls?
options: 36 rows, 18 of them exact duplicates of the first run
18 rows, because to_sql() silently skips rows that already exist
36 rows, but SQLite automatically removes the duplicates on read
An error on the second call, because the table already exists
questions.explain: if_exists="append" has no concept of "already loaded" — it just appends whatever rows it's handed, every single call. Running this twice against the same 18-row clean_df leaves 36 rows in the table, 18 of them exact duplicates — exactly the duplicate-row problem Lesson 37 uses to motivate upserting on order_id instead.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of Lesson 38's config-driven run_pipeline() in the correct order.
items: Load settings from config.json into a config dictionary
Extract only rows newer than the current watermark from the source CSV
Clean the extracted rows (fill missing names, drop invalid quantities)
Upsert the cleaned rows into the warehouse, keyed on order_id
Write the new watermark value, based on the max order_date actually loaded
questions.explain: Lesson 38 wires Lessons 32-37 together in exactly this order: load config first so nothing downstream is hardcoded, extract only new rows using the current watermark, clean them, upsert them for idempotency, and only after the load succeeds advance the watermark — updating it before the load would silently skip those rows forever if the load then failed.

questions.prompt: Match each ETL pipeline role, per Lesson 32, to what it's actually responsible for.
right: Writing the result to its destination
Cleaning and reshaping data into the form the target expects
Calling each stage in order and passing one stage's output to the next
Pulling raw data from a source
questions.explain: Extract pulls raw data from a source like orders.csv. Transform cleans and reshapes it into the form the target expects. Load writes the result to its destination. The orchestrator's only job is calling the three stages in order and passing each one's output to the next — it contains no cleaning logic or file-handling details of its own.

questions.chapter: Logging, Testing, Error Handling and Automation
questions.prompt: What are Python's five logging levels, in order from least to most severe?
options: DEBUG, INFO, WARNING, ERROR, CRITICAL
INFO, DEBUG, WARNING, CRITICAL, ERROR
TRACE, DEBUG, INFO, ERROR, CRITICAL
DEBUG, WARNING, INFO, ERROR, CRITICAL
INFO, WARNING, ERROR, DEBUG, CRITICAL
DEBUG, INFO, ERROR, WARNING, CRITICAL
questions.explain: The logging module's five levels run DEBUG < INFO < WARNING < ERROR < CRITICAL. Setting level=logging.INFO means debug() calls are silently skipped while info() and everything more severe still logs — that's how levels filter noise without deleting any of the logging calls themselves.
questions.distractorExplain: Option D is the closest-sounding wrong answer because it includes all five correct level names, just reordered — but WARNING actually sits between INFO and ERROR in real severity, not before INFO. Getting the order right matters because it's exactly what determines which messages get filtered out at a given configured level.

questions.chapter: Logging, Testing, Error Handling and Automation
questions.code:
logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO, format="%(asctime)s [%(levelname)s] %(message)s")
logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)

logger.debug("Row 4521: raw value before cleaning = '  42.0 '")
logger.info("Extracted 10,482 rows from orders.csv")
questions.prompt: What actually gets logged when this runs?
options: Only the info() message — the debug() call is silently skipped, because the configured level is INFO
Both messages print, since debug() and info() are both below ERROR
Only the debug() message, because it was called first
Neither message prints, because basicConfig() needs level=logging.DEBUG to log anything at all
questions.explain: level=logging.INFO means anything below INFO — which is exactly where DEBUG sits — is silently skipped, while INFO and anything more severe still prints. Only the logger.info() call produces output here; the logger.debug() call is filtered out by the configured level, not by call order.

questions.chapter: Logging, Testing, Error Handling and Automation
questions.prompt: Select every true statement about pytest, per Lesson 40.
options: pytest discovers tests automatically by filename (test_*.py) and function name (test_*), with no registration step
pytest.raises(ValueError) is how you assert that a block of code is expected to raise that exception
A validation function that's only ever tested with good input can hide a bug in its rejection path
Once a test for the 'good' input case passes, there's no need to also test the function's rejection cases
assert fails the test only if the expression evaluates to exactly the string "False"
questions.explain: pytest auto-discovers tests by the test_*.py / test_* naming convention, no registration required. pytest.raises() is the mechanism for asserting a function is supposed to raise a specific exception. Testing only the good case can hide a bug in the exact rejection path a real pipeline leans on to catch bad data — which is why Lesson 40 insists on testing both sides, not treating the good-case test as sufficient. assert passes when its expression is truthy, not specifically the string "False" — a falsy value of any kind fails it.

questions.chapter: Logging, Testing, Error Handling and Automation
questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: `os.environ["DB_PASSWORD"]` raises a ________ immediately if that environment variable isn't set, rather than silently continuing with no password at all.
questions.explain: os.environ["KEY"] raises a clear KeyError immediately if the variable isn't set — unlike os.environ.get("KEY", default), which quietly falls back to a default. Lesson 43 uses the first form for required settings like a database password specifically so a missing value fails loudly instead of proceeding with nothing.

questions.prompt: No action is called after this. What actually happens when these two lines run?
options: Nothing is read or computed yet — filter() and groupBy() are transformations that just record the plan
Spark immediately scans the full dataset to apply the filter
An error, because groupBy() can't be called on the result of filter() without an action in between
grouped becomes a DataFrame containing the filtered, grouped rows, ready to print
questions.explain: filter() and groupBy() are transformations — Spark just records what was asked for, without doing it yet. Only an action like .show(), .count(), or .collect() actually triggers Spark to read the data and run the recorded plan. Chaining transformations with no action afterward means nothing has actually run against real data at all.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: .show(), .count(), and .collect() are called ________ in PySpark — they're what actually triggers Spark to read the data and run the recorded transformation steps.
questions.explain: Actions are what actually trigger execution in PySpark's lazy-evaluation model. Transformations like filter() and groupBy() only build up a plan; nothing runs until an action like .show(), .count(), or .collect() is called.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about groupBy().agg() and joins in PySpark, per Lesson 46.
options: alias() renames an aggregated column so it's not left with an awkward default name like avg(fare_amount)
A left join between trips and the zone lookup table keeps every trip row, even if its location ID has no match in the lookup table
Grouping by more than one column means each unique combination of those columns becomes its own group
A trip with no matching zone in a left join is dropped from the result entirely
questions.explain: Without alias(), an aggregated column would be named something awkward like avg(fare_amount); alias() renames it to something clean, like avg_fare. A left join keeps every row from trips, filling in null for pickup_zone/pickup_borough when a location ID has no matching zone — it never drops that trip row. Grouping by VendorID and passenger_count together means each unique combination becomes its own group, the same way multi-column groupby works in pandas.

questions.prompt: Put these stages of the mini capstone pipeline, per Lessons 47-48, in the correct order.
items: Extract the trips and zone lookup files, logging the row count of each
Clean the trips data by filtering out non-positive fares and distances
Join the cleaned trips to the zone lookup table to get real zone names
Aggregate by pickup zone to compute trip count and average fare
Validate the result's row count and value ranges before trusting it
questions.explain: The capstone pipeline runs extract -> clean -> transform (join) -> aggregate -> load, and Lesson 48 adds one more step after the pipeline finishes: validating the output's row count and value ranges, because a pipeline finishing with no exceptions is not the same as its output being correct.
